body:
One point:

I vaguely remember using `resize(0)` in a performance sensitive part specifically because it implies no de-allocation (and I see from the comments someone else doing similar). `clear()` is rather more vague as a function name, I wouldn't put it past some well meaning soul to come along in future and change it to de-allocate to "save memory".

This is arguably over-future proofing, but I've learned the hard way to never underestimate the ability of noobs to come in and break performance sensitive code in the future, particularly with containers. :grinning:
(Same can be true of bounds checking in containers.)

That said I'm not against it, just we need to beware anyone changing the `clear()` function in future, and by renaming in this way, this distinction is lost (unless comments are added in place).

> I vaguely remember using `resize(0)` in a performance sensitive part specifically because it implies no de-allocation (and I see from the comments someone else doing similar). `clear()` is rather more vague as a function name, I wouldn't put it past some well meaning soul to come along in future and change it to de-allocate to "save memory".

This PR does not change any behavior.: `clear()` already de-allocates for `CowData` types. This is notably different from `std::vector` and `PacketBuffer` where `clear` does not shrink the array.

I do think this is somewhat of a semantic clash, so we may want to rename `clear` into something else like `destroy` to emphasize it deallocates the array. In a future PR 😅

> This PR does not change any behavior.

The concern is that although the PR doesn't change behaviour, information as to _intent_ may be lost in translation.

> : clear() already de-allocates for CowData types.

That is a bit more problematic, because now we have confirmed different containers with different expectations for `clear()`.

One way around this might be to e.g. add a default `bool` argument to the `LocalVector::clear()` function as to whether to free up the memory, defaulting to the current behaviour (not freeing memory), and setting the `bool` explicitly in these cases which are converted from `resize(0)`.

e.g.:
```
void clear(bool p_free_memory = false)
{
...
}
```

> > This PR does not change any behavior.
> 
> The concern is that although the PR doesn't change behaviour, information as to _intent_ may be lost in translation.
> > : clear() already de-allocates for CowData types.
> 
> That is a bit more problematic, because now we have confirmed different containers with different expectations for `clear()`.
> One way around this might be to e.g. add a default `bool` argument to the `LocalVector::clear()` function as to whether to free up the memory, defaulting to the current behaviour (not freeing memory), and setting the `bool` explicitly in these cases which are converted from `resize(0)`.
> 
> e.g.:
> 
> ```
> void clear(bool p_free_memory = false)
> {
> ...
> }
> ```

I think, generally, we're on to something here. We found a semantic clash (`clear` with deallocation vs `clear` to just remove elements but keep the capacity the same).
Still, the function we have right now is `clear`, translating to `x.clear(); x.shrink_to_fit()` in other C++ APIs. As such, _all callers_ of `clear` should be treated like they intend to destroy the array. If any existing callers intended to simply deallocate the elements, but keep the capacity the same, their intention has already been lost, long before this PR.
Closing this because it's very outdated, and `clear()` has now already been simplified.
